grammar: וַיָּרָץ and וַיֹּאמֶר are wayyiqtol forms: the vav-consecutive carries the narrative from one action to the next.
הַגְמִיאִינִי is a hifil imperative, feminine singular, addressed to the girl, with the suffix ־נִי; the speaker is the servant.
לִקְרָאתָהּ: ל with the infinitive construct of קָרָא and the suffix ־הּ forms the set phrase 'to meet her'.
The zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר divides the narrative from the speech that follows.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the word is the term for swallowing (לְשׁוֹן גְּמִיעָה), which in Old French is humer.
Radak: the word means as הַשְׁקִינִי, 'give me to drink'.
Rashi: the servant ran because he saw the water rising to meet her, citing Bereshit Rabbah.
Radak: he ran because he saw she was beautiful, and he relied on God for his questions.

וַתְּמַהֵר and וַתֹּרֶד: a piel and a hifil wayyiqtol, both with the feminine subject, mark the quick succession of her actions.
כַּדָּהּ עַל־יָדָהּ: the jar and the hand both carry the feminine suffix ־הּ; the phrase is 'her jar upon her hand'.
וַתַּשְׁקֵהוּ: a hifil wayyiqtol with the object suffix ־הוּ; the verb carries 'give to drink' without a noun for the drink.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וַתֹּרֶד means 'from her shoulder' (מֵעַל שִׁכְמָהּ): she lowered the jar from her shoulder. The English keeps the verse's 'upon her hand'.
Radak: she called him 'my lord' because she did not know who he was, and she quickly hastened to give him water.

grammar: The etnaḥta on לְהַשְׁקֹתוֹ closes the first clause; the revia on וַתֹּאמֶר begins the speech.
גַּם comes before its object, as in Hebrew, 'also for your camels'; the English moves 'too' to the end of the speech.
עַד אִם כִּלּוּ לִשְׁתֹּת: the temporal clause 'until' with אִם; the piel perfect כִּלּוּ has the camels as subject.
The piel כִּלּוּ is used without an object, 'they had finished' (drinking), and the infinitive לִשְׁתֹּת names the act.
segments.note: The English 'too' renders גַּם as 'also'. The speech is one verse long and closes within it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: אִם here serves as אֲשֶׁר ('which'): until they have had enough, which is the end of their drinking.
Radak: 'until they have finished drinking'; or אִם stands for אֲשֶׁר, 'until they are able to drink'. The English takes the first.
Sforno: she waited to speak until he had finished drinking, following the rule that one does not speak at a meal in case the windpipe goes down the wrong way.

context: Camels drink large quantities of water after a long journey; the verse's own detail (until they had finished drinking) shows why the drawing took long.

grammar: וַתְּעַר, וַתָּרָץ, וַתִּשְׁאַב: three wayyiqtols in a sequence of quick actions, pouring, running, drawing.
עוֹד אֶל־הַבְּאֵר: 'again to the well'; the verb רוּץ returns from 24:17.
לִשְׁאֹב is an infinitive construct of שָׁאַב with no stated object; the English keeps the bare verb.
לְכָל־גְּמַלָּיו: the construct לְכָל, 'all of', with the plural גְּמַלָּיו and the suffix 'his'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וַתְּעַר means scattering (נְפִיצָה), like the Mishnaic word for pouring from one vessel into another.
Rashi: the שֹׁקֶת is a hollow stone from which the camels drink.
Radak: she poured it into the trough, the place where the animals are watered.
Sforno: the well is in front of the spring from which the animals drink.

context: A שֹׁקֶת was a trough or basin from which animals drank; Rashi glosses it as a hollow stone.

grammar: וְהָאִישׁ מִשְׁתָּאֵה לָהּ מַחֲרִישׁ: two participles, hitpaʿel and hifil, describe the man's state; the English supplies 'was'.
לָדַעַת: the infinitive construct of יָדַע with ל of purpose, 'in order to find out'.
הַהִצְלִיחַ: the interrogative ה with the hifil perfect; the question ends in אִם לֹא, 'or not'.
The zaqef gadol on מַחֲרִישׁ divides the verse; the silluq on לֹא closes it.
segments.note: The LORD: יְהֹוָה is rendered in the usual English form; the decisions give no rule for the bare name. Ibn Ezra's 'like משתומם' and Rashi's 'amazed' agree on the sense of מִשְׁתָּאֵה, so the English takes it.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: מִשְׁתָּאֵה is like מִשְׁתּוֹמֵם, 'astonished', from the root of שָׁאוּ עָרִים (Isaiah 6:11).
Ibn Ezra: לָהּ means 'for her sake' (like בִּשְׁבִילָהּ); the ת belongs to the hitpaʿel, and the word cannot come from שָׁתָה ('drink').
Rashi: he was amazed and startled, seeing that his errand was close to success, but he did not know whether she was of Abraham's family.
Rashi: מִשְׁתּוֹמֵם עָלֶיהָ, 'amazed at her'.
Radak: he was amazed at her, seeing how quickly she acted, and kept silent without asking whose daughter she was until the camels had drunk.
Radak: the question 'whether the LORD had made his way prosper, or not' means whether she is a good woman of Abraham's family or not. The English keeps the plain sense of the question.
Sforno: he was astonished at the great eagerness with which she did the kindness.

grammar: וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר: a wayyiqtol of הָיָה with a temporal clause, 'it came to pass when'.
נֶזֶם זָהָב, בֶּקַע מִשְׁקָלוֹ, עֲשָׂרָה זָהָב מִשְׁקָלָם: the material is named, then the weight, with the suffix on מִשְׁקָל.
וּשְׁנֵי צְמִידִים עַל־יָדֶיהָ: the dual יָדֶיהָ is 'her two hands'; the bracelets are plural.
The verse has no verb for putting the ring or the bracelets on her: the placing is not stated (see Ramban in the commentary).
segments.note: The shekel is the text's unit of weight; the English gives 'shekel' as the measure, not as coin. The ring and bracelets are given by weight, not by piece.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: a נֶזֶם is worn in the nose or in the ear; this one is the nose-ring, hanging from a cord tied on the forehead.
Ibn Ezra: בֶּקַע means half (a shekel), from the root of נִבְקַע, 'split'.
Ibn Ezra: צְמִידִים comes from the root of צָמִיד, a tied cord (Numbers 19:15); there is one bracelet on each hand, so two, and their shape is known.

Ramban: the verse omits the act of giving. He takes it that the ring and bracelets were taken for her, and that after she named her family he set the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her hands, as he had said to them. The English does not adopt this.
Radak: he gave her the ring after asking whose daughter she was; the narrative tells it in that order, the question first and then the gift. The verse's order is kept in the English.
Radak: בֶּקַע is half a shekel; he put it on her nose, as the servant later tells (24:47), and likewise the two bracelets on her hands.
Radak: 'ten of gold' is as the Targum renders it.
Rashi: an allusion to the half-shekel of Israel for the head.
Rashi: an allusion to the two tablets joined together.
Rashi: an allusion to the ten commandments.
Sforno: this was some time after she had finished watering; he saw she asked nothing, and her deeds were all full kindness.

apparatus: Ramban reads the verse as eliding the placing of the ring and bracelets; the English keeps the verse's own words.
context: The shekel was a unit of weight; gold and silver were weighed in shekels before coined money came into use in the region. The text gives the weight of the gold, not the number of pieces.
Nose-rings were worn in the ancient Near East; the text puts this one on the nose (Ibn Ezra: hung from a cord tied on the forehead).

grammar: בַּת־מִי אַתְּ: a nominal clause, 'whose daughter are you', with the independent pronoun אַתְּ, feminine.
הַגִּידִי נָא לִי: a hifil imperative, feminine singular, 'tell me, please', addressed to the girl.
הֲיֵשׁ בֵּית־אָבִיךְ מָקוֹם לָנוּ לָלִין: the interrogative ה with יֵשׁ, 'is there'; the construct 'house of your father'.
לָלִין is an infinitive with ל of purpose; the parse is qal, and Ibn Ezra reads it as hifil.
segments.note: The form לָלִין (with yod) is kept as the pack's qal infinitive construct, so the sense path is Qal 1. Ibn Ezra's hifil reading is recorded below, not adopted, because the morphology data is not overridden.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: לָלִין is from the heavier, added binyan (hifil, the causative), since the light stem is לָלוּן. The English keeps the qal the parse gives.
Radak: the form with yod is hifil and the form with waw is qal, and the two are one in meaning here: the request and the answer both concern the lodging of the men and the camels.
Radak: the verb is transitive, like 'they lodge naked' (Job 24:7): he asked for a place for the camels to lodge, and she answered that there is a place for them in her father's house as well.
Rashi: לִין is a noun for a single lodging, and the form לָלוּן, which she uses, means several lodgings.
Rashi: after he had given her the ring, he asked her, trusting in Abraham's merit that the Holy One made his way prosper.

apparatus: The form לָלִין (with yod): the pack's parse is qal infinitive construct; Ibn Ezra and Radak read a hifil (causative). The qal sense is used, and the hifil reading is recorded in the commentary.

בַּת בְּתוּאֵל אָנֹכִי: a nominal clause with the independent pronoun אָנֹכִי, 'I', at the end.
בֶּן־מִלְכָּה אֲשֶׁר יָלְדָה לְנָחוֹר: a relative clause with אֲשֶׁר; the subject of יָלְדָה is Milcah.
The zaqef gadol on מִלְכָּה closes the first part of the answer; the silluq on לְנָחוֹר closes the verse.

commentary.summary: Rashi: she answered the first question first and the last question last.
Radak: she answered the first question; Milcah and Nahor were known, so she said all of this.
